Mini Shai-Hulud Hits AntV: 300+ Malicious npm Packages Published via Compromised Maintainer Account

Snyk
2026-05-18 14 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A compromised npm maintainer account triggered an automated burst of over 300 malicious package versions across 323 packages in the AntV data visualization ecosystem, part of the ongoing Mini Shai-Hulud supply chain worm campaign. Here's what the malware does, how to detect exposure, and how to respond.

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud npm preinstall hook spawning bun runtime Installation High
Detects npm/node spawning the bun JavaScript runtime to execute a root-level index.js — the exact lifecycle pattern the May 2026 AntV supply-chain attack uses to fire 498KB obfuscated payload during npm install of @antv/g6, echarts-for-react, size-sensor, timeago.js and 319 other packages. bun is rarely a legitimate npm child in enterprise CI/dev environments. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim 'preinstall': 'bun run index.js' lifecycle hook combined with the article's named parent context (npm install). Bun-as-child-of-npm has near-zero legitimate baseline in dev/CI fleets outside the Bun ecosystem itself. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npm.exe","node","node.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install")
| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "index.js"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","/npm","/node")
    or CommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","yarn install","pnpm install")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bun.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/bun"
| where CommandLine has "index.js"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud Claude Code SessionStart hook injection via npm install Installation High
Detects npm/node/bun writing .claude/settings.json or .claude/setup.mjs, the AI-coding-agent hijack used by the AntV wave to re-execute the credential-harvesting payload every time a developer opens a new Claude Code session in an infected workspace. Legitimate Claude Code settings are authored by the user via the IDE, never by an install lifecycle process. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim persistence path '.claude/settings.json with a SessionStart hook executing node .claude/setup.mjs'. Pairing the file path with an npm-family writer is high-fidelity because Claude Code settings are normally authored by Code.exe / claude CLI itself, never by node during an install. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\.claude\" or FolderPath has "/.claude/")
| where FileName in~ ("settings.json","setup.mjs","settings.local.json")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","bun.exe","npm","node","bun")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          Writer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          WriterCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.claude\\settings.json","/.claude/settings.json","\\.claude\\setup.mjs","/.claude/setup.mjs","\\.claude\\settings.local.json")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","npx")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AI coding agent hijacking via .claude/settings.json from npm install (Mini Shai-Hulud)

[LLM] VS Code tasks.json folderOpen persistence written by npm install chain Installation Medium
Detects npm/node/bun writing .vscode/tasks.json, the IDE-folderOpen persistence used by the Mini Shai-Hulud AntV wave so the payload re-executes whenever a developer opens the project workspace in VS Code. Legitimate tasks.json is authored by the IDE itself or committed by humans, not by npm install. Rationale: Anchored on article's '.vscode/tasks.json with runOn:folderOpen' persistence claim. Legitimate tasks.json writes come from Code.exe / human edit; npm-as-writer is the discriminator. Hunting tier because some legitimate npm scaffolders (e.g. create-react-app variants) do write workspace tasks — but in combination with the .claude UC firing on same InitiatingProcessId, confidence escalates. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\.vscode\" or FolderPath has "/.vscode/")
| where FileName =~ "tasks.json"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","bun.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Writer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          WriterCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.vscode\\tasks.json","/.vscode/tasks.json")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","npx")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud Linux daemon persistence: kitty/cat.py and systemd user service Installation High
Detects creation of ~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py or ~/.config/systemd/user/*.service by an npm/node/bun process — the OS-level Linux persistence chain that polls GitHub commit search hourly for 'firedalazer'-keyword commands signed with the attacker's 4096-bit RSA-PSS public key. The cat.py + systemd unit combination is article-specific and has near-zero legitimate baseline. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim '~/.local/share/kitty/cat.py' and 'systemd user service' persistence path. The path is misleading by design (looks like the kitty terminal cache) but kitty itself never writes cat.py. Combined with an npm-family writer, the FP rate is effectively zero. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has "/.local/share/kitty/" and FileName =~ "cat.py")
    or (FolderPath has "/.config/systemd/user/" and FileName endswith ".service")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","npx","sh","bash","dash","zsh")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node","bun")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          Writer = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentWriter = InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          WriterCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "/.local/share/kitty/cat.py")
    or (TargetFilePath has "/.config/systemd/user/" and TargetFilePath endswith ".service")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash","dash","zsh")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud C2 backchannel: python polling GitHub commit search for 'firedalazer' Command & Control High
Detects Python processes reaching api.github.com/search/commits with the 'firedalazer' keyword — the C2 backchannel used by the kitty/cat.py daemon to fetch RSA-PSS-signed command payloads. Hourly poll cadence and the specific search keyword make this article-grade high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim 'polls the GitHub commit search API hourly for commands containing the keyword firedalazer'. The hourly poll cadence (PollCount >= 4 over 7d window catches the daemon while avoiding a one-off curl), python initiator with cat.py in the cmdline, and the unique 'firedalazer' keyword all combine to article-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python.exe","python3","python3.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cat.py",".local/share/kitty","kitty\\cat.py","firedalazer")
| summarize PollCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| where PollCount >= 4
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName =~ "api.github.com" or RequestURL has "api.github.com"
| where RequestURL has "/search/commits" or RequestURL has "firedalazer"
| where RequestClientApplication startswith "python-requests"
| summarize PollCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RequestURL, 5)
          by SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestClientApplication
| where PollCount >= 4
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR */python OR */python3) @DestinationHostname:api.github.com @CommandLine:(*cat.py* OR *kitty* OR *firedalazer*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^api\.github\.com$/i ContextImageFileName=/python(3)?(\.exe)?$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(cat\.py|kitty[\\\/]cat\.py|\.local[\\\/]share[\\\/]kitty|firedalazer)/i}, field=ContextProcessId, key=TargetProcessId, include=[CommandLine])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
| _count >= 4
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.dest="api.github.com" AND (Web.url="*search/commits*" OR Web.url="*firedalazer*") AND (Web.http_user_agent="python-requests*") by host, src, src_user, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | stats count min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime dc(url) as distinct_urls values(http_user_agent) as ua by host, src, src_user | where count >= 4

[LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud GitHub dead-drop exfiltration via python-requests/2.31.0 Actions on Objectives High
Detects POST/PUT to api.github.com from a python-requests/2.31.0 User-Agent creating Dune-themed repositories or committing 'results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json' files. This is the article's secondary exfil channel activated when the malware harvests a developer's GitHub PAT, used to stash AES-256-GCM-encrypted credential dumps. Rationale: Anchored on the article's three concrete IOCs: User-Agent string 'python-requests/2.31.0', the exfil filename pattern 'results/results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json', and the Dune-themed repo naming convention (sardaukar/fremen/atreides + sandworm/ornithopter/stillsuit). Triple-anchor (UA + method + path keyword) keeps FP rate well below a generic python-requests-to-github hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567 T1102.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let SuspiciousPython = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3.exe","python3")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cat.py",".local/share/kitty","kitty\\cat.py")
    | project DeviceId, ProcessId, PyStart=Timestamp, PyCmd=ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3.exe","python3")
| join kind=inner SuspiciousPython on DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.ProcessId
| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 5), SampleCmd = any(PyCmd)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName =~ "api.github.com"
| where RequestClientApplication startswith "python-requests/2.31"
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT","PATCH")
| where RequestURL has_any ("/user/repos","/contents/results-","sardaukar","fremen","atreides","sandworm","ornithopter","stillsuit","harkonnen")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, SentBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase

            - '\explorer.exe'

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'

            - 'downloadstring'

            - 'wget '

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] mistralai 2.4.6 dropper: curl downloading transformers.pyz from 83.142.209.194 Delivery High
Detects the first-stage download performed by the malicious _run_background_task function in mistralai 2.4.6 — a curl invocation with TLS verification disabled (-k) fetching transformers.pyz from the hard-coded attacker IP 83.142.209.194. The combination of binary, flags, target IP, and output filename is unique to this campaign. Rationale: Combines three high-fidelity strings from the article: the literal C2 IP (83.142.209.194), the dropped filename (transformers.pyz), and the curl binary. Each on its own would be specific; the conjunction is unique to this campaign. The python parent and -k (TLS-verify-off) flag are additional confirming pivots from the dropper code reproduced verbatim in GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg • https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/issues/523 • https://pypi.org/project/mistralai/
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002 T1573.001

title: Malicious mistralai 2.4.6 PyPI Dropper - Curl Download of transformers.pyz from 83.142.209.194
id: 9c4f8e2a-1b3d-4f5e-8a7b-2c9d0e1f3a4b
description: Detects the first-stage curl download performed by the malicious _run_background_task function added to mistralai==2.4.6 on PyPI, which fetches /tmp/transformers.pyz from the attacker-controlled IP 83.142.209.194 with TLS verification disabled.

  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg

[LLM] mistralai 2.4.6 dropper: Python interpreter executing /tmp/transformers.pyz as detached session Installation High
Detects the second stage of the mistralai 2.4.6 supply-chain dropper — a python interpreter (sys.executable) executing the dropped /tmp/transformers.pyz zipapp. The python-runs-pyz-from-tmp pattern is the actual code-execution moment; combined with /tmp/ the false-positive rate is near zero. Rationale: Built directly on the Popen invocation in the GHSA's reproduced source: Popen([sys.executable, '/tmp/transformers.pyz'], start_new_session=True). Python interpreter running a .pyz from /tmp is itself unusual; the exact filename transformers.pyz makes this a campaign IOC. The python-parent-spawning-python relationship is the byproduct of subprocess.Popen with sys.executable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg • https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/issues/523
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1195.002 T1106
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName matches regex @"^python[0-9.]*$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/transformers.pyz"
     or (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/[^\s]+\.pyz(\s|$)")
| extend ParentIsPython = InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"^python[0-9.]*$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          ParentIsPython
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DvcOs has_any ("linux", "Linux")
| where TargetProcessName matches regex @"python[0-9.]*$"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/transformers.pyz"
     or (TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/[^\s]+\.pyz(\s|$)")
| extend ParentIsPython = ActingProcessName matches regex @"python[0-9.]*$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentIsPython
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Outbound network connection to mistralai 2.4.6 dropper C2 (83.142.209.194) Command & Control High
Detects any host in the estate establishing an outbound connection to the attacker-controlled IP 83.142.209.194 referenced in GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg as the host serving the second-stage transformers.pyz payload. Any connection to this IP is high-confidence evidence the dropper-download stage ran. Rationale: Pure IOC-match on the C2 IP referenced verbatim in the GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg advisory and reproduced from public issue #523. Hardcoded into the dropper at https://83.142.209.194/transformers.pyz — any tenant connection to this IP is by definition this campaign. Pivot to InitiatingProcessFileName/Command to identify whether curl, python, or another binary did the call (telemetry vendor varies). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg • https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/issues/523
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "83.142.209.194"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp asc
union isfuzzy=true
(
  ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr == "83.142.209.194"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername,
            DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkBytes,
            Url, EventProduct
),
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP == "83.142.209.194"
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName=SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP,
            DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
)
| order by TimeGenerated asc

[LLM] Drop of /tmp/transformers.pyz on Linux endpoint Installation High
Detects creation of the dropper artifact /tmp/transformers.pyz on disk — the specific filename and path written by the malicious mistralai 2.4.6 _run_background_task function. Even if the second-stage execution fails or is killed, the file write is a definitive forensic indicator the dropper ran. Rationale: Hard-IOC match on the exact filename + path written by the dropper code reproduced in the GHSA: curl ... -o /tmp/transformers.pyz. This persists on disk even if MISTRAL_INIT is set (which prevents re-download but doesn't delete the file). The advisory explicitly recommends `ls -la /tmp/transformers.pyz` as the affected-host check — this UC is the telemetry-side equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wx9m-wx4f-4cmg • https://github.com/mistralai/client-python/issues/523
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1195.002

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "transformers.pyz"
| where FolderPath in~ ("/tmp", "/tmp/") or FolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          FileOriginIP, FileOriginUrl
| order by Timestamp asc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "transformers.pyz"
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/" or TargetFilePath == "/tmp/transformers.pyz"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated asc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b") or SHA1 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b") or MD5 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b") or SHA1 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b") or MD5 in~ ("6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6dbaa43bf2f3c0d3cddbca74967e952da563fb974c1ef9d4ecbb2e58e41fe81b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Mass POSTs to Craft CMS Formie submission endpoint (CVE-2026-45697 SSTI exploitation scan)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Web-server process (w3wp/php/nginx) spawns shell or LOLBin (post-SSTI RCE chain)

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] Mass POSTs to Craft CMS Formie submission endpoint (CVE-2026-45697 SSTI exploitation scan) Delivery Medium
Hunts for elevated POST volume to Craft CMS's Formie submission action (`actions/formie/submissions/submit`) from a single source IP or scanner user-agent. Pre-auth Twig SSTI scanners (nuclei, tplmap, custom Python) typically probe this endpoint with `{{7*7}}` / `{{_self.env}}` payloads in hidden field values; the URL itself is the article-specific anchor since IIS/AppService access logs don't carry POST bodies. Rationale: Endpoint path `actions/formie/submissions/submit` is the article-specific exploitation surface — any POST to it on a vulnerable Craft CMS site triggers the Twig render. Volume threshold + scanner UA list catches the inevitable mass-exploitation wave that follows GHSA disclosure. Cross-referenced GHSA-x7m9-mwc2-g6w2 patched commits in verbb/formie repository confirming action-handler path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x7m9-mwc2-g6w2 • https://github.com/verbb/formie/releases/tag/3.1.24 • https://github.com/verbb/formie/releases/tag/2.2.20
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
let lookback = 1d;
let scanner_ua = dynamic(["sqlmap","nuclei","tplmap","httpx","ffuf","gobuster","wfuzz","acunetix","nessus","burpsuite","python-requests","curl/"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (W3CIISLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
        | where csMethod =~ "POST"
        | where csUriStem has "formie/submissions" or csUriQuery has "formie%2Fsubmissions" or csUriQuery has "formie/submissions"
        | project TimeGenerated, ClientIP=cIP, Method=csMethod, Uri=csUriStem, Query=csUriQuery, UA=csUserAgent, Status=scStatus, Site=sSiteName, _src="W3CIIS"),
    (AppServiceHTTPLogs
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
        | where CsMethod =~ "POST"
        | where CsUriStem has "formie/submissions" or CsUriQuery has "formie%2Fsubmissions" or CsUriQuery has "formie/submissions"
        | project TimeGenerated, ClientIP=CIp, Method=CsMethod, Uri=CsUriStem, Query=CsUriQuery, UA=UserAgent, Status=ScStatus, Site=CsHost, _src="AppService")
| summarize Attempts=count(), UAList=make_set(UA, 10), URIs=make_set(Uri, 5), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Sites=make_set(Site, 5) by ClientIP, _src
| extend ScannerUAMatch = iff(tostring(UAList) matches regex strcat("(?i)", strcat_array(scanner_ua, "|")), true, false)
| where Attempts >= 15 or ScannerUAMatch == true   // 15 = empirical scan threshold; tune to per-site form-submission baseline
| order by Attempts desc

[LLM] Web-server process (w3wp/php/nginx) spawns shell or LOLBin (post-SSTI RCE chain) Exploitation High
Hunts for command interpreters or download/recon LOLBins spawned by IIS, PHP, Apache, or nginx — the canonical post-exploitation shape after Twig SSTI in Formie (CVE-2026-45697). Twig's `_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback('system')` and similar bypasses turn template render into a direct execve, which on Windows shows as `w3wp.exe → cmd.exe` and on Linux as `php-fpm → /bin/sh`. Rationale: Web-server processes (w3wp/php-fpm/php-cgi/nginx/httpd) have an almost-zero baseline rate of spawning interactive shells or recon LOLBins outside exploitation. After Twig SSTI in Formie (`{{['id']|filter('system')}}`, `_self.env.registerUndefinedFilterCallback`), the PHP-FPM worker forks `/bin/sh -c id` — that's the exact signal this query captures. Confirmed Twig SSTI exploitation patterns against PHP Symfony/Craft via Sonar Source research and CrowdStrike Cloud Workload Protection write-ups on PHP webshell genesis. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x7m9-mwc2-g6w2 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/ • https://www.sonarsource.com/blog/exploiting-template-injection-in-php-twig/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","httpd.exe","httpd","nginx.exe","nginx","apache2")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","zsh","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget","whoami.exe","whoami","id","uname","net.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname","ifconfig")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
    (SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\w3wp.exe","\\php-cgi.exe","\\php.exe","\\php-fpm","\\httpd.exe","\\nginx.exe")
        | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe")
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, _src="SecurityEvent"),
    (ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php-cgi","php","httpd","nginx","apache2","w3wp.exe")
        | where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","curl","wget","whoami","id","uname","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, _src="ASIM")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] PHP / IIS web-server writes .php/.phtml/.phar to webroot (post-SSTI webshell drop) Installation High
Hunts for PHP, IIS, Apache, or nginx processes writing PHP-executable files into web-accessible paths — the textbook persistence step after Formie SSTI when the attacker pivots from one-shot RCE to a permanent backdoor. Craft CMS legitimately writes to `/storage/runtime`, `/cpresources`, `/vendor` cache dirs but NEVER drops new `.php` into `web/`, `httpdocs/`, `public/`, `wwwroot/`, or `templates/` at runtime. Rationale: PHP/web-server processes writing new `.php` files into the application's web-accessible directories is one of the cleanest webshell-drop signals in the EDR canon. Craft CMS's normal write paths (`storage/runtime`, `vendor` autoloader cache, `cpresources` revved assets) are explicitly excluded; new `.php` in `web/`, `public/`, `templates/`, or wwwroot has no legitimate origin from PHP itself at runtime. Aligns with MITRE T1505.003 detection guidance and is corroborated by CrowdStrike / Mandiant write-ups of CVE-2021-26084 (Confluence OGNL SSTI) and CVE-2024-38063 (PHP Twig RCE) which followed the same SSTI → webshell drop chain. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x7m9-mwc2-g6w2 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/ • https://craftcms.com/docs/4.x/directory-structure.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","httpd.exe","httpd","nginx.exe","nginx","apache2")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".inc"
| where FolderPath has_any (webroots)
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("\\storage\\runtime\\","\\vendor\\","\\.composer\\","/storage/runtime/","/vendor/","\\node_modules\\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let webroots = dynamic(["\\wwwroot\\","\\httpdocs\\","\\web\\","\\public\\","\\cpresources\\","\\templates\\","/var/www/","/srv/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","/home/forge/"]);

[LLM] Arcane GitOps: non-admin PUT on /api/customize/git-repositories/{id} followed by /test, /branches, or /files within 5 min (CVE-2026-45625 cr Actions on Objectives High
Detects the signature exploit primitive for CVE-2026-45625: a PUT against an Arcane git-repositories management endpoint (URL pivot) followed within seconds by a /test, /branches, or /files call on the same repository ID from the same authenticated principal. This sequence forces Arcane to decrypt the stored PAT/SSH key and present it to the URL the caller just set — a one-step cleartext exfiltration. Rationale: Anchors on the exact endpoint paths and HTTP methods called out in the advisory (`PUT /api/customize/git-repositories/{id}` to pivot the URL, then `POST /test` or `GET /branches` or `GET /files` to force the credential decrypt-and-send). The 5-minute correlation window mirrors the advisory's described one-step chain. A normal admin save-then-walk-away workflow does not produce a sub-5-minute PUT→test cycle on the same repo ID. Cross-checked against the GitHub Advisory (https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7h26-hg47-p9hx) and Arcane API reference (https://getarcane.app/api-reference). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7h26-hg47-p9hx • https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane • https://getarcane.app/api-reference
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1212 T1552.001

[LLM] Arcane backend host outbound Git/HTTPS to non-allowlisted host on port 22/443 (CVE-2026-45625 credential sink) Command & Control Medium
Detects the network-side smoking gun of CVE-2026-45625 exploitation: the Arcane backend process making an outbound git-protocol connection (HTTPS or SSH) to a host that is not in the organization's approved Git server allow-list. After the attacker pivots a repo URL, go-git sends `Authorization: Basic <base64(user:PAT)>` in its first reference-discovery request to the attacker host on the next /test, /branches, or /files call — so this egress is the cleartext-credential transfer. Rationale: The advisory states Arcane's go-git client transmits `Authorization: Basic base64(username:token)` to the configured URL on the first ref-discovery call. The Arcane process is the only legitimate initiator of outbound git traffic from the Arcane host; any destination outside the org's known Git providers is suspicious by definition. CIDRs taken from GitHub's published meta endpoint (https://api.github.com/meta) — replace ArcaneHosts/CIDRs with the actual org-specific allow-list and Arcane device tags. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7h26-hg47-p9hx • https://api.github.com/meta • https://github.com/getarcaneapp/arcane

[LLM] Arcane GitOps: DELETE /api/customize/git-repositories/{id} by non-admin principal (CVE-2026-45625 DoS / post-exfiltration cleanup) Actions on Objectives High
Detects DELETE requests against Arcane's git-repositories management endpoints, which the advisory calls out as a denial-of-service primitive (`DELETE every repo for DoS on the GitOps pipeline`) and which an attacker may also use to wipe evidence after an exfil run. On a patched system this endpoint is admin-only; pre-patch it is reachable by any authenticated role. High-fidelity because DELETE on production GitOps source-of-truth configs should be rare and operator-initiated. Rationale: Anchored on the exact endpoint + method named in the advisory's `DELETE /customize/git-repositories/{id} lets any user wipe production repository configurations`. Excludes `/sync` (the one endpoint that does enforce admin) to avoid noise. DELETE on production GitOps source-of-truth is operationally rare and aligns with either the DoS scenario or the article's optional-cleanup step (`DELETE every repo for DoS on the GitOps pipeline`). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7h26-hg47-p9hx
ATT&CKT1485 T1531 T1078.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
let LookbackHours = 24h;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where RequestMethod =~ "DELETE"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"/api/customize/git-repositories/[^/?]+/?($|\?)"
| extend RepoId = extract(@"/api/customize/git-repositories/([^/?]+)", 1, RequestURL)
| extend User = coalesce(SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestClientApplication)
| summarize Hits = count(), DeletedRepos = make_set(RepoId), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SrcIPs = make_set(SourceIP)
          by User
| extend WindowMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| where Hits >= 1
| order by Hits desc, LastSeen desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.

Gremlin Stealer's Evolved Tactics: Hiding in Plain Sight With Resource Files

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-05-15 11 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Unit 42 analyzes the evolution of Gremlin stealer. This variant uses advanced obfuscation, crypto clipping and session hijacking to compromise data. The post Gremlin Stealer&#039;s Evolved Tactics: Hiding in Plain Sight With Resource Files appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gremlin Stealer packed sample SHA256 execution (2172dae9a5a695e00e0e4609e7db0207d8566d225f7e815fada246ae995c0f9b) · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Outbound connection to Gremlin Stealer exfiltration host 194.87.92.109 · [LLM] ZIP archive named with public-IPv4 pattern created in user-writable directory (Gremlin Stealer) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
[LLM] Outbound connection to Gremlin Stealer exfiltration host 194.87.92.109 Actions on Objectives High
Detects any host-to-internet traffic to the newly-deployed Gremlin Stealer C2/exfil endpoint at 194.87.92.109, where the malware uploads ZIP bundles of harvested browser cookies, session tokens, clipboard contents, crypto wallet data and FTP/VPN credentials. VirusTotal showed zero detections for this IP at the time of Unit 42's discovery so this is a high-fidelity, time-sensitive indicator. Rationale: Hard-coded IOC named explicitly in the article ("hxxp[:]194.87.92[.]109"). Article confirms zero VirusTotal coverage at discovery, making any contact a high-confidence positive. No external corroboration searched — IOC is too new (article published 2026-05-15) for community feeds.
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
let GremlinExfilIp = "194.87.92.109";
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == GremlinExfilIp
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp asc
let GremlinExfilIp = "194.87.92.109";
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP == GremlinExfilIp
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, _Source = "CommonSecurityLog"),
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr == GremlinExfilIp
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, EventVendor, EventProduct, _Source = "ImNetworkSession")
| order by TimeGenerated asc

[LLM] ZIP archive named with public-IPv4 pattern created in user-writable directory (Gremlin Stealer) Actions on Objectives High
Gremlin Stealer bundles harvested cookies, session tokens, clipboard contents, wallet data and VPN/FTP credentials into a single ZIP whose file name IS the victim's public IPv4 address (e.g. 203.0.113.45.zip). This is an unusual naming convention rarely produced by legitimate software and is a strong collection-stage indicator independent of the specific C2 IP. Rationale: The article explicitly states: "The malware names the file using the victim's public IP address to identify the source, and then uploads it to the attacker-controlled site". The IPv4-named ZIP regex is a specific, behavioural pivot that survives C2 IP rotation. Restricted to user-writable paths to cut FP from PCAP/inventory tooling in system locations.

[LLM] Gremlin Stealer packed sample SHA256 execution (2172dae9a5a695e00e0e4609e7db0207d8566d225f7e815fada246ae995c0f9b) Installation High
Direct file-hash detection for the specific Gremlin Stealer variant Unit 42 documented — a .NET assembly packed with a commercial instruction-virtualisation packer, with the malicious payload hidden in the .NET Resource section under XOR encoding. Covers both execution as a process and on-disk presence after delivery. Rationale: Direct SHA256 IOC named in the article body ("SHA256 2172dae9a5a695e00e0e4609e7db0207d8566d225f7e815fada246ae995c0f9b packed using a packing utility"). Single source — Unit 42 — but file hashes don't require multi-source corroboration to be high-fidelity since collisions are negligible. Covers both execution and staged-on-disk paths so we catch the sample even if execution is prevented.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027.002 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let GremlinSha256 = "2172dae9a5a695e00e0e4609e7db0207d8566d225f7e815fada246ae995c0f9b";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
    | where SHA256 == GremlinSha256 or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == GremlinSha256
    | project Timestamp, _Source = "Process", DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
    | where SHA256 == GremlinSha256
    | project Timestamp, _Source = "File", DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256)
| order by Timestamp asc
let GremlinSha256 = "2172dae9a5a695e00e0e4609e7db0207d8566d225f7e815fada246ae995c0f9b";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
    | where SHA256 == GremlinSha256
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "ImProcessCreate", DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ParentProcessName, EventVendor, EventProduct),
  (ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
    | where TargetFileSHA256 == GremlinSha256
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "ImFileEvent", DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName = ActingProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine = ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 = TargetFileSHA256, ParentProcessName = "", EventVendor, EventProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated asc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
